title: After
contentNote: This chapter touches on how the war stayed with Henry in later life, including the memories that troubled him when he was old.
summary: In short: Henry came home in December 1918 and married Nell on 28 December. He drove one of Yeovil's first charabancs and later long-distance lorries, kept prize canaries and budgies, rose through the Buffaloes to the Roll of Honour, and raised three children. He had been gassed, and his breathing was never right again. He never talked about the war, but it stayed with him. He died on 18 January 1963.

scenes.title: Home
scenes.intro: Henry landed at Hull on 4 December 1918. Just over three weeks later, on 28 December, he married Ellen Mary Taylor, known as Nell, at the parish church in Maperton, Somerset.

context.text: Returning prisoners landed at Hull, Leith or Dover, went by train to reception camps such as Ripon, and were given two months' leave, £2 and a printed letter of welcome from the King. Many came home still in prison-camp clothes.

Leaving the army, a man could take a suit of plain clothes or 52 shillings and sixpence, and was insured against being out of work for up to 26 weeks. In the Class Z Reserve he could be recalled "in the event of a grave national emergency".
context.source: The Long, Long Trail, Demobilisation and discharge

context.text: Discharged to the Class Z Reserve on 13 March 1919.

Married at Maperton parish church on 28 December 1918, by licence. Henry, a bachelor, gave his rank as Lance Corporal and his home as Maperton; Nell, a spinster, lived in Yeovil. Both fathers, Arthur Bowles and Henry Taylor, were labourers.

photos.caption: Henry and Nell on their wedding day, 28 December 1918. Henry is still in uniform: he stayed a soldier, on prisoner-of-war leave, until March 1919.
photos.alt: Henry in army uniform and peaked cap, with a moustache, standing beside Nell in a wide-brimmed hat and dark coat.
photos.credit: Family photograph

photos.caption: Henry and Nell's marriage certificate, 28 December 1918. He gave his rank as "Soldier, L. Corp": a Lance Corporal, still in the army just over three weeks after landing back in England.
photos.alt: A green-bordered handwritten certificate headed Certified Copy of an Entry of Marriage, with a red one-penny King George V stamp at the foot. A full transcript follows.
photos.credit: Family papers
transcript: The Parish Church, in the Parish of Maperton, in the County of Somerset. Entry number 105
Henry John Bowles, aged 25, bachelor. Rank or profession: Soldier, L. Corp. Residence: Maperton
Ellen Mary Taylor, aged 25, spinster. Residence: Yeovil
According to the rites and ceremonies of the Church of England, by licence
Harry Taylor and Ethel Joyce Bowles (the handwriting of both names is hard to read)
Cyril White, Rector of Maperton, 28th December 1918
photos.transcriptNote: The register gives Henry's age as 25. By his birth certificate he was 24, six months short of 25. Small slips like this were common.

photos.caption: About 1919 to 1920: Henry and Nell, seated, with baby Gilbert. Behind Henry stand his parents, Arthur Bowles and his wife; behind Nell, her brother George Taylor; on the right, Nell's parents, Mr and Mrs Taylor.
photos.alt: A sepia family group in a garden: a young man and a young woman holding a baby in a long white gown sit in front of two older couples and a younger man.
photos.credit: Family photograph

photos.caption: The King's letter to returning prisoners: "The Queen joins me in welcoming you". Does the family still have Henry's?
photos.alt: A framed printed letter with a royal crest.
photos.credit: Image: IWM (EPH 4582)

paras: Home. Mother didn't say anything at all, just held on to me in the doorway till Father said let the boy in, he's letting the cold in. Then she cried, and then she made tea, the way she did the day I told her I'd joined.
The little ones aren't little. Some of them are taller than me now. They look at me like they're waiting for me to say something about it. I don't.
They've given us two months' leave, two pounds, and a letter from the King. I've put the King's letter in the drawer.
And I'm to be married. Nell and me, this month. I can hardly believe it's me writing that, in this same book. The same pencil, near enough. A month ago I was behind wire in Germany.
I'll be a married man for Christmas.
basis: Landed at Hull on 4 December 1918 (casualty record).
He married Ellen Mary Taylor on 28 December 1918 at Maperton parish church, giving his home as Maperton and his rank as Lance Corporal (their marriage certificate).
Returning prisoners were given two months' leave, a £2 payment and a printed letter of welcome from King George V (Great War Forum accounts).
His parents, Arthur Bowles and his wife, both lived into their nineties (Angela Wright's memoir).

paras: Finished with the Army. Class Z Reserve, they call it, which means they can have me back if there's another war, and God help us if there is.

Back on the land. The work's the same as it ever was, the horses and the plough and the weather, and it's a comfort, it's the only comfort some days. A furrow either runs straight or it doesn't. Nobody gets killed if it doesn't.
I don't sleep so well. Nell says I talk in the night. I tell her it's nothing. The cold gets on my chest too, since the gas, and some mornings I'm coughing before I'm out of bed.

This is the last page in this book I'm going to write. It's done its job. I'll put it away with the King's letter and the medals when they come, and I'll not talk about any of it, not to anybody. Some things you carry so the others don't have to.
God bless them all. Ours and theirs.
basis: Discharged to the Class Z Army Reserve on 13 March 1919 (casualty record).
Class Z men went back to civilian life but could be recalled "in the event of a grave national emergency" (The Long, Long Trail).

He was a farm hand after the war; a photograph is described of him with baby Gilbert on a plough behind a horse. He "never talked to anybody about the War", and late in life he was troubled by memories of it (Angela Wright's memoir).
"Grandad had been gassed during WWI in France and since then had always had problems breathing" (Memories of Grandad). When and where is not recorded.
The notebook itself is imagined, and so is everything Henry says here.

scenes.title: The farm and the lorries
scenes.intro: Henry and Nell had three children: Gilbert Henry Arthur, Joyce, whom her youngest brother Bill always called "Joycie One-Name", born on 22 July 1921, and William George, known as Bill, born in 1924. These memories are their granddaughter Angela's, with some from Joyce's grandson Tristan.

stories.title: On the mower
stories.body: Angela Wright's memoir remembers a photograph of Henry on a plough with baby Gilbert on his lap. Here it is. In fact it shows a horse-drawn grass mower, with two heavy horses in harness. Where and when it was taken is not known.
stories.source: Angela Wright's memoir, page 1

stories.title: The charabanc
stories.body: Henry drove for the rest of his working life, and never took a driving test. A charabanc was an open motor coach: rows of wooden benches on a lorry chassis, with solid tyres and no roof but a folding canvas hood. In Yeovil, Bird Brothers, the firm Henry drove for, ran charabanc trips to Cheddar Gorge and Bournemouth in the 1920s. Later he became a long-distance lorry driver.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright; Yeovil's History, Charabanc excursions
stories.quote: one of the first men in Yeovil to drive a Charabanc
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: Bird Brothers and British Road Services
stories.body: In 1924 the family moved to 67 Southville, Yeovil, the year their youngest, Bill, was born. Henry drove for Bird Brothers, and later long-distance lorries for British Road Services. The 1939 Register lists him at 67 Southville as a lorry driver, "heavy worker".
stories.source: Tristan Cobb's family research

stories.title: Twelve miles an hour
stories.body: In 1924 two policemen timed his lorry over a measured furlong near Blandford: 16 miles 928 yards an hour, when the limit for a heavy lorry was 12. Henry said he was sorry, and told the constable that lorries ought to be made to carry speedometers. He was fined ten shillings. In 1935 he was fined £1 for going over 20 miles an hour.
stories.source: Newspaper reports, from Tristan Cobb's family research

stories.title: A working man
stories.body: In 1931 a policeman at Broadwindsor stopped his lorry, carrying the sections of a building laid flat, 9 feet wide, too wide to pass another lorry. Henry wrote to the magistrates pleading guilty. He had not meant it, he said, and hoped they would be lenient. The case was dismissed with a caution.
stories.source: Newspaper report, 17 July 1931, from Tristan Cobb's family research
stories.quote: only a working man with a wife and three children

stories.title: Knight of the Road
stories.body: For all that, he was given a "Knight of the Road" award for his driving, and he had never taken a driving test.
stories.source: Tristan Cobb's family research

stories.title: "Hello then"
stories.body: On holiday in a hired car, if another driver did something wrong, Henry wound down the window and said "hello then". Asked if he knew them, he said: "No, but they know what I mean."
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: Half a crown
stories.body: When his daughter Joyce was home on leave from the ATS, Henry bet her half a crown that she couldn't reverse his lorry and trailer into a space. "And he had to pay up as she did it perfectly."
stories.source: Angela Wright's memoir, page 1

stories.title: Pack it away
stories.body: The story goes, from Henry's daughter Joyce, that if she or her brothers came home and left anything lying about, like shoes kicked off after a dance, Henry would go and wake them up and tell them to put it away: their mother was not their servant.
stories.source: Joyce Bush's memory, from Tristan Cobb's family research

stories.title: Burnt to a crisp
stories.body: It is said Henry liked his bacon burnt to a crisp, just as his great-grandson Tristan does.
stories.source: Tristan Cobb's family research

stories.title: The bird hospital
stories.body: Henry turned an old shed into an aviary for canaries and budgies, with two cages kept for sick birds: his "bird hospital". Seed and water were measured out exactly. He showed his birds in Yeovil and usually came home with certificates. He was a member of the cage bird association in Yeovil, and built the aviary in his back garden.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright; Tristan Cobb's family research
stories.quote: It was special to do that with him.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: The Bowles day out
stories.body: Twice the whole family hired two coaches for a day out, once to Badbury Rings near Wimborne: all twelve brothers and sisters, their husbands and wives, children and grandchildren, with crates of beer in the boot. Henry hardly relaxed all day. He was worried how his brothers would behave after a drink. He enjoyed a beer or cider himself, but "would never get drunk".
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: The Buffaloes
stories.body: Henry was a member of the Royal Antediluvian Order of Buffaloes for more than twenty years. The next scene tells that story through the jewels he was given.
stories.source: Angela Wright's memoir, page 1; Tristan Cobb's family research

photos.caption: A charabanc outing in 1920 or 1921: the men's club of St Mark's, Plumstead, in south-east London. Not Henry's charabanc, but the kind of vehicle he drove in Yeovil, with its bench seats, solid tyres and folding hood.
photos.alt: A sepia postcard of an open charabanc, registration XB 8568, parked by a wooden fence in front of a church. About forty passengers in straw boaters, flat caps and summer hats sit in rows on its benches, with the driver at the wheel at the front. It has solid tyres on spoked metal wheels and a folded canvas hood at the back.
photos.credit: Postcard, 1920 to 1921, from the collection of Mark Crombie. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

photos.caption: Henry with little Gilbert on his lap, on a horse-drawn mower behind two heavy horses, about 1920.
photos.alt: Two large dark working horses in harness pull a mowing machine through long grass; a man in a hat and waistcoat sits on the seat holding a small child in white.
photos.credit: Family photograph

photos.caption: The three children, about 1930. From the left: Bill, the youngest, Joyce and Gilbert.
photos.alt: A studio photograph of two boys in jackets and long socks either side of a girl in a pale dress.
photos.credit: Family photograph

photos.caption: Henry and Nell with their grown-up children, before the children went off to the Second World War. Standing, from the left: Bill, Joyce and Gilbert.
photos.alt: A studio portrait of an older couple seated, the woman in round glasses, with two young men in suits and a young woman in pearls standing behind them.
photos.credit: Family photograph

photos.caption: Henry, crouching on the left, beside his British Road Services lorry, NLJ 958, after a crash. The front of the cab is smashed. When and where it happened is not known.
photos.alt: A badly damaged lorry with a crushed cab and broken windscreen, its front wheels in a grassy ditch. The registration plate reads NLJ 958. A man in a cap crouches at the bottom left, beside the front of the lorry.
photos.credit: Family photograph, from Tristan Cobb's family research
photos.with: Bird Brothers and British Road Services

photos.caption: Angela and her grandad, Henry, with one of his birds, in the 1950s. He kept canaries and budgies, and showed them in Yeovil.
photos.alt: A man in a sleeveless pullover kneels in a vegetable garden beside a small girl. Together they hold a bird cage standing on a wooden stool, with a terrace of houses behind them.
photos.credit: Family photograph, lent by Angela Wright

scenes.title: The Buffaloes
scenes.intro: For more than twenty years after the war, Henry belonged to the Royal Antediluvian Order of Buffaloes, a friendly society of working men known as the Buffs. The jewels he was given, engraved on the back with names and dates, are now kept by his granddaughter Angela. Each degree has its own colour: green, royal blue, red and light blue. Read together, the jewels tell the story of his life in the lodge.

panels.title: A society of working men
panels.text: The Royal Antediluvian Order of Buffaloes began in London in 1822 among theatre stagehands. "Antediluvian" means "from before the Flood", a joke about how old it claimed to be. Lodges met in rooms above pubs and in clubs, raised money for charity, and looked after members and their families when times were hard.
panels.source: Royal Antediluvian Order of Buffaloes, Wikipedia

panels.title: Four degrees
panels.text: Each degree has its own colour, worn on the sash and the jewel's ribbon. A new member, a Brother, is in the first degree and wears green. To reach the second, Certified Primo (C.P.), he sits an examination in front of his fellow members, showing he understands the Order's ceremonies and laws, and then wears royal blue. After at least three years, if his lodge thinks him worthy, his name goes to the Provincial Grand Lodge of South Somerset and on to Grand Lodge, and he is raised to the third degree, Knight of the Order of Merit (K.O.M.), in red. After at least five more years he can be added to the Roll of Honour kept by Grand Lodge: the fourth and highest degree, in light blue, whose members are addressed as "Sir". Henry reached all four.
panels.source: Michael, a source in the Buffaloes in South Somerset, writing to Angela Wright, October 2026; Royal Antediluvian Order of Buffaloes, Wikipedia

panels.title: Business, then harmony
panels.text: A lodge meeting began with its formal business, led by the Worthy Primo, the highest of the lodge's 14 offices. Then it moved into "harmony": songs, jokes and turns from the members. Most offices changed hands every month. Three, including Waiter, were held for twelve months at a time.
panels.source: Michael, a source in the Buffaloes in South Somerset, writing to Angela Wright, October 2026; Royal Antediluvian Order of Buffaloes, Wikipedia

panels.title: The motto
panels.text: Many of the jewels carry the Order's Latin motto, Nemo mortalium omnibus horis sapit: "No man is wise at all times." The Roll of Honour jewel has its own: Palma non sine pulvere, "No prize without effort."

stories.title: The broken pipe
stories.body: Among Henry's things is a white clay pipe with buffalo horns and the letters R.A.O.B. moulded on the bowl. Its stem is broken. Every new member of the Buffaloes takes part in an initiation ceremony that involves breaking a clay pipe. Nobody can now say for certain, but this may be the pipe from Henry's own first night in the lodge, kept for the rest of his life.
stories.source: The pipe, kept by the family; Hackney Museum, RAOB clay pipe

stories.title: 18 June 1928: a Brother
stories.body: The first bar on Henry's knighthood jewel gives the date he joined: his first degree, 18 June 1928. He had turned 34 four days earlier, and was nearly ten years home from the war: a lorry driver with a wife and three children at 67 Southville, Yeovil. As a new Brother he would have worn green.
stories.source: Henry's Buffaloes jewels, kept by his granddaughter Angela Wright

stories.title: 7 December 1931: Certified Primo
stories.body: Three and a half years later Henry passed the examination for his second degree. St John's Lodge, No. 4652, gave him a silver jewel on the royal blue ribbon of a Certified Primo, with PRIMO on the bar. The engraving on the back calls him by the name his friends used: Harry.
stories.quote: Presented to Bro Harry Bowles by the St Johns Lodge No 4652
stories.who: Engraved on the back of the jewel
stories.source: Henry's Buffaloes jewels, kept by his granddaughter Angela Wright; Michael, a source in the Buffaloes in South Somerset, writing to Angela Wright, October 2026

stories.title: Never missing a meeting
stories.body: Several of Henry's jewels were given for attendance. Trinity Lodge, No. 6620, which still meets today, added a bar for the years 1931, 1932 and 1933. Selwyn Lodge, No. 7206, since closed, and St John's Lodge each gave him a jewel too, for services rendered and for regular attendance. He seems to have belonged to more than one lodge at once.
stories.source: Henry's Buffaloes jewels, kept by his granddaughter Angela Wright; Michael, a source in the Buffaloes in South Somerset, writing to Angela Wright, October 2026

stories.title: A gift for the orphans
stories.body: The Buffaloes ran their own orphanage at Grove House in Harrogate, from 1927 until 1947, when the new welfare state took over. Henry gave money to it, and to other good causes, and was presented with a Donor jewel showing the orphanage building. It names him H. J. Bowles C.P., so he gave it between 1931 and 1936.
stories.source: Henry's Buffaloes jewels, kept by his granddaughter Angela Wright; Grove House, Harrogate, Wikipedia

stories.title: 1935: the Silver Jubilee
stories.body: In 1935 King George V and Queen Mary celebrated 25 years on the throne. Selwyn Lodge marked it with a jewel showing the King and Queen, hanging from a bar of buffalo horns, engraved for "Bro. H. Bowles C.P." The man who had answered the King's call in 1915 now wore the King's face on his lodge ribbon.
stories.source: Henry's Buffaloes jewels, kept by his granddaughter Angela Wright

stories.title: 23 April 1936: a Knight
stories.body: On St George's Day 1936 Selwyn Lodge made Henry a Knight of the Order of Merit, the third degree, on the red ribbon of a knight. His lodge had put his name forward, through the Provincial Grand Lodge of South Somerset, to Grand Lodge. The back of the gilt cross carries the longest engraving of all his jewels. It says the honour was given in appreciation of his services to the Buffaloes, and of their regard for him as a man and a brother.
stories.quote: their regard for him as a man and a brother
stories.who: Engraved on the back of his knighthood jewel
stories.source: Henry's Buffaloes jewels, kept by his granddaughter Angela Wright; Michael, a source in the Buffaloes in South Somerset, writing to Angela Wright, October 2026

stories.title: Waiter, 1940
stories.body: In the first winter of the Second World War, with all three of his children grown up, St John's Lodge gave "Bro. H. Bowles K.O.M." a jewel for services rendered, dated 6 December 1940. Its bar reads WAITER. The Waiter fetched the brothers' drinks, and it was one of only three lodge offices held for a whole year rather than a month.
stories.source: Henry's Buffaloes jewels, kept by his granddaughter Angela Wright; Michael, a source in the Buffaloes in South Somerset, writing to Angela Wright, October 2026

stories.title: Father and son
stories.body: Henry's eldest son, Gilbert Henry Arthur Bowles, followed him into St John's Lodge. Gilbert's own knighthood cross, on the same crimson ribbon as his father's, has bars for his first degree on 22 December 1940 and his second on 14 October 1942. On 19 August 1946 he was "Exalted" to the third degree, as his father had been ten years before. Gilbert died of peritonitis in January 1948, less than eighteen months later. His jewel stayed with his father's.
stories.source: Henry's Buffaloes jewels, kept by his granddaughter Angela Wright; Angela Wright's family research

stories.title: Treasurer, 1952
stories.body: By the 1950s Henry was trusted with the lodge's money. His last dated jewel, on a red and green ribbon, names him Treasurer of St John's Lodge and was presented for services rendered in 1952. The Order's records show he reached high office in the Buffaloes in South Somerset, and he would have served as Worthy Primo, the head of his lodge. Family memory remembers him as head of the lodge opposite the Salvation Army in Southville, Yeovil.
stories.source: Henry's Buffaloes jewels; Michael, a source in the Buffaloes in South Somerset, writing to Angela Wright, October 2026; Angela Wright's memoir, page 1; Tristan Cobb's family research

stories.title: The Roll of Honour
stories.body: Henry's highest honour was the Roll of Honour, the fourth degree, with its star-shaped jewel, its crown and a light blue sash. His name was added to the roll kept by Grand Lodge, and from then on he was addressed in the lodge as "Sir". The jewel is not dated, but the Roll of Honour came at least five years after his knighthood, so no earlier than 1941.
stories.source: Henry's Buffaloes jewels; Michael, a source in the Buffaloes in South Somerset, writing to Angela Wright, October 2026

stories.title: Days out with the Buffs
stories.body: The Buffaloes were a family affair too. In the 1950s the lodge hired a coach for an outing, and Henry took his granddaughter Angela. His parents' diamond wedding party, in December 1953, was held at the R.A.O.B. Club in Yeovil.
stories.source: Family photograph; diamond wedding newspaper report, 1953

paras: Joined the Buffs tonight. One of the drivers has been on at me for a year to come along, and Nell said go on, it'll do you good to be among the men of a evening instead of out in the shed with they birds.
I won't write down what goes on. That's for the lodge. But they gave me a pipe, and I've brought it home, and I'm keeping it.
It's a funny thing. A room full of men, and half of them were out there same as me, and not one of them said a word about it. We sang instead, and I laughed till I coughed.
First time I've felt like one of a company since the Army. I didn't know I'd missed it.
basis: His first degree in the Buffaloes was taken on 18 June 1928 (the bar on his knighthood jewel).
Initiation into the Buffaloes involves breaking a clay pipe; lodge meetings move from business into "harmony", with songs and turns (Hackney Museum; Wikipedia).
Henry kept a broken R.A.O.B. clay pipe, which the family still has. He kept canaries and budgies, and his chest was never right after the war (Memories of Grandad).
The conversation with Nell and every word of the entry. Who brought Henry into the Buffaloes is not known.
entries.disclosure: AI imagined journal, written for Henry from his Buffaloes jewels and his family's memories

paras: Our Gilbert was raised to Knight tonight, at St John's. Exalted, they call it. I stood up at the back with the others and I'll own I had to look at the floor for a bit.

Ten years since they did the same for me. He's a man now, been through his own war, and we come home together after, father and son, walking down Southville in the dark, and neither of us said much. Didn't need to.
Nell asked how it went. I said he did us proud. She knew what I meant.
basis: Gilbert Bowles was "Exalted" at St John's Lodge, No. 4652, on 19 August 1946; Henry had been made a Knight of the Order of Merit in April 1936 (their jewels).
Henry and Nell lived at 67 Southville, Yeovil. Gilbert, Joyce and Bill all went off to the Second World War (family photographs and research).
Whether Henry was there that night is not known. The walk home and every word are imagined.
entries.disclosure: AI imagined journal, written for Henry from his Buffaloes jewels and his family's memories

photos.caption: A Buffaloes outing in the 1950s, gathered in front of the coach. Henry is on the far right of the back row. Angela is the fourth child from the left in the front row, with her mother Joyce standing behind her and her father Cyril behind Joyce.

photos.credit: Family photograph, lent by Angela Wright

asks.q: Who were the Buffaloes, and why did so many old soldiers join societies like it?

scenes.title: Grandad
scenes.intro: When Angela's father was called up by the Navy for the Korean War and her mother went back to work, Angela spent her days with her grandparents, Henry and Nell, at their house in Southville. "Those were just lovely days."

stories.title: Flat cap and boots
stories.body: Outdoors he always wore a flat cap, boots and a belt, with his sleeves rolled up in summer. On the beach at Weymouth he sat in a deckchair in shoes, socks, long trousers, shirt and cap. Just occasionally he took off his shoes and socks, rolled up his trousers and paddled.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
stories.quote: I can't even remember him in trunks or going for a swim.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: The hand and the belt
stories.body: Henry was a strong disciplinarian. Angela remembers: "Grandad would tell me that I would have his belt. That Never happened. Just a movement of hand was all that was needed."
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
stories.quote: Grandad never showed anything but love.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: Queen and princess
stories.body: Angela spent almost fourteen years growing up with her grandad, Henry, in her life.
stories.source: Angela Wright's memoir, page 1
stories.quote: I was always Grandad's queen and when Sandra came along she was his princess.

stories.title: Report day
stories.body: Henry and Nell lived halfway between school and home, so on school report day Angela would pop in and persuade them to open her report first, "so I would know what the marks were before I got home. Very helpful at times."
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

photos.caption: Henry and Nell walking arm in arm in Weymouth, Henry in his flat cap.
photos.alt: An older couple walk towards the camera along a seaside promenade with flags behind them. The man wears a flat cap, jacket and pullover; the woman, in round glasses, wears a long coat over a pale dress.
photos.credit: Family photograph, from Tristan Cobb's family research

photos.caption: Angela and her grandparents, Henry and Nell, on the beach at Weymouth in the early 1950s. Henry is in shirt, braces and long trousers, just as Angela remembers him at the seaside.
photos.alt: On a crowded beach, an older woman in round glasses and a flowered dress and a man in an open-necked shirt and braces sit in deckchairs either side of a small fair-haired girl with a bow in her hair. Beach huts and seafront buildings are behind them.
photos.credit: Family photograph, lent by Angela Wright

photos.caption: Angela with all three of her grandparents, at the bungalow in Poole of Henry's sister Winnie, in the 1950s. Standing, from the left: Henry, Mrs Bush (her other grandmother) and Nell. Kneeling: Winnie and Angela.
photos.alt: Five people outside a pebble-dashed bungalow. Standing are a man in shirt and braces, a very elderly woman in a dark dress holding a walking stick, and a woman in round glasses and a flowered dress. Kneeling in front are a smiling woman in a flowered dress and a young girl in a checked dress with a white collar.
photos.credit: Family photograph, lent by Angela Wright

photos.caption: Angela and her grandad, Henry, on the grass at the Nothe, Weymouth, in about 1962, when she was 13. His cap lies on the grass beside him.
photos.alt: A white-haired man in a shirt with rolled sleeves and dark trousers sits on a grassy slope beside a teenage girl in a sun hat, blouse and full skirt. A pale cap and a dark jacket lie on the grass beside him.
photos.credit: Family photograph, lent by Angela Wright

scenes.title: Nell
scenes.intro: To Angela, her grandparents Henry and Nell came "as a package". Nell, Henry's wife, deserves her own page.

stories.title: In service
stories.body: Before she married, Nell had been in service. She made sure her granddaughter Angela learned to lay a table properly, every day, not just on special occasions.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
stories.quote: I still try to do that today.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: The motorbike
stories.body: Nell sat on a backless chair by the sink to do the vegetables. Angela sat behind with her arms round Nell's waist, and it became their motorbike, taking sharp corners and racing to the crossroads.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
stories.quote: Things you do for your granddaughter.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: The Army
stories.body: Nell went to the Salvation Army, and took her granddaughter to the Sunday meetings, to the Corps on holiday in Weymouth, and to her midweek ladies' services. On Saturdays it might be fish and chips at Thorpes, with bread and butter, and grace before they ate.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
stories.quote: It was Grandma that taught me about Jesus and how to trust Him.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: Sunday dinner
stories.body: Sunday lunches were a family time, with Henry and Nell's son Bill, who lived with them. Nell was a good cook.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: The only time
stories.body: Nell died of cancer on 5 June 1961, aged 67. That morning, Angela called in as usual. Henry was alone in the garden.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright; Tristan Cobb's family research
stories.quote: As I walked down the path I could see he was crying. That was the only time I saw him cry.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

scenes.title: What he carried
scenes.intro: Henry never talked about the war. But it never quite left him.

stories.title: The silence
stories.body: Like many men of his generation, he kept the war to himself.
stories.source: Angela Wright's memoir, page 10
stories.quote: A part that he didn't talk about, because I think it was too raw for him to do so.

stories.title: What the family knew
stories.body: The stories of him in the Great War were few. The family knew he had been a prisoner, and that he brought the walking stick home. Joyce's husband, Cyril Bush, always believed Henry had served in the Somerset Light Infantry. Nobody mentioned the Wiltshire Regiment, where he spent most of his war. He did tell them he had been gassed, which is why they went to Weymouth for the sea air.
stories.source: Tristan Cobb's family research

stories.title: Gassed
stories.body: Every winter he had bronchitis and chest infections. His army record doesn't mention gas, so we don't know when it happened. His Wiltshire battalion met mustard gas near Ypres in July 1917, though Henry may only have rejoined it that August. When he died in 1963, his death certificate gave acute and chronic bronchitis as the cause.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright; his death certificate
stories.quote: Grandad had been gassed during WWI in France and since then had always had problems breathing.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: Weymouth
stories.body: The sea air and the flat Promenade at Weymouth were good for his chest, so for years the family took their holidays there, in a flat on the Nothe side of the harbour, with their neighbours from Southville. Fishermen gave them spare fish.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
stories.quote: On days when grandad couldn't walk too far he would have a chair on the harbour and enjoyed chatting to those passing by.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: The barbed wire
stories.body: Towards the end of his life Henry grew less tolerant; Angela's piano lessons at his house lasted two weeks, because he couldn't stand the noise. And he began to see things that weren't there.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
stories.quote: Asking me to get the barbed wire off him and stop people running all over him.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: Understanding
stories.body: Angela only understood what Henry had been living through many years later, when she read Sebastian Faulks's novel Birdsong.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
stories.quote: At the time I had no idea what he meant or wanted.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: What we know now
stories.body: Doctors in Henry's time called it shell shock. Today we would recognise much of it as post-traumatic stress: a real injury to the mind, which can return in old age. Many veterans of both world wars were troubled by memories late in life.
stories.source: Science Museum, Wounded: from shell shock to PTSD

asks.q: What was a gas attack like?
What were the mines, and who dug them?

paras: Bad night again. My chest like a sack of wet sand, and the dreams.
It's always the wire. I'm caught on it and I can't get free, and they're coming over, all of them, running, and nobody sees me. I wake up and Bill's in the doorway saying Dad, Dad, it's all right.
The little one was here today practising her piano, and I couldn't bear it, God forgive me. Every note went right through me. I told her mother it was the noise. It wasn't the noise.
Forty-odd years and I never told a soul. I thought if I kept it shut away it would stay there. It doesn't stay. It waits.
Still. I've had a good life, better than most of them got. The garden, the birds, the grandchildren running in and out. That's what it was for. That's what it was all for.
basis: Late in life he asked his granddaughter to "get the barbed wire off him and stop people running all over him". Her piano lessons at his house lasted two weeks because he couldn't stand the noise. He was gassed, and had breathing problems for the rest of his life. His son Bill lived with him (Memories of Grandad).
He never talked about the war: "it was too raw for him" (Angela Wright's memoir).
Every word. These are thoughts written for Henry, not things he said. He never told anyone.

scenes.title: A happy note
scenes.intro: Henry died at Yeovil General Hospital on 18 January 1963, aged 68. His granddaughter Angela was two days short of her fourteenth birthday.

stories.title: A happy note
stories.body: Henry and Nell had 3 children, 4 grandchildren and 10 great-grandchildren, and when Angela wrote her memoir there were 10 great-great-grandchildren, and counting.
stories.source: Angela Wright's memoir, page 10
stories.quote: Grandad's life did end on a happy note

stories.title: Together again
stories.body: Henry was buried with Nell at Yeovil Cemetery, in grave B3817. In March 1963 his affairs were settled by Joyce and Bill, then a confectionery salesman. He left £382 4s.
stories.source: Probate calendar and burial record, from Tristan Cobb's family research

stories.title: Their sons
stories.body: Henry and Nell outlived one of their sons. Gilbert died of peritonitis on 21 January 1948, and never saw his own son, John. Bill never married, lived with his parents, and died on 28 January 1968.
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright

stories.title: Thank you
stories.source: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
stories.quote: Grandma and Grandad, you were such a wonderful example to me. Thank you.
stories.who: Memories of Grandad, by Angela Wright
